title: What If You Could Smell a Disease Years Before Doctors Found It? One Woman Can

scenes.text: What if you could smell an illness years before any doctor could find it? One woman can.
She noticed her husband's scent change to something musty. Twelve years later, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.
Scientists tested her with twelve T-shirts: six worn by patients, six by healthy people. She picked out every patient, plus one healthy volunteer.
One mistake. Except eight months later, that volunteer was diagnosed with Parkinson's too.
The smell is in sebum, the oil on our skin. A team at the University of Manchester worked with her to track down what changes in it.
In 2022 they turned it into a skin swab that gives a result in three minutes, about 95 percent accurate in the lab. A test that began with one person's nose.

description:
What if a person could smell a disease long before it was diagnosed? A woman with an unusually sensitive nose noticed her husband's smell change more than 12 years before he was diagnosed with Parkinson's.
In a test with twelve T-shirts she identified all six patients and flagged one healthy volunteer, who was diagnosed about eight months later. Working with her, University of Manchester researchers traced the odour to changes in sebum and in 2022 described a skin-swab test using mass spectrometry that takes about three minutes and was about 95 percent accurate under laboratory conditions. It is still being studied in larger trials.
